title: Routing, switching, BGP and latency
scopeHtml: Scope: switches vs routers, routing tables, BGP and internet structure, latency vs distance. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Switch vs router vs hub
notes.html:
A switch connects devices inside one network using MAC addresses. A router connects different networks using IP addresses. A hub (obsolete) just repeats every bit to every port.

A switch learns: when a frame arrives on port 3 from MAC aa:bb, it records aa:bb -> port 3 in its MAC table. Later frames to aa:bb go only to port 3. Unknown destination or broadcast: flood out all other ports.

$ bridge fdb show br0       # Linux bridge MAC table
aa:bb:cc:00:00:01 dev eth1 master br0
aa:bb:cc:00:00:02 dev eth2 master br0

Worked example. A 48-port gigabit switch has a backplane of 96 Gbps (48 x 1 Gbps x 2 for full duplex) and can forward all ports at line rate. A hub would share 1 Gbps across everyone, with collisions.

Industry examples. Data center switches from Arista, Cisco and Juniper, and in-house ones by Google and Meta (white-box switches running SONiC). Home "routers" are really a router, switch, Wi-Fi AP, NAT and DHCP server in one box.

Everyday analogy. A switch is an office mail clerk who knows every desk; a router is the post office that sends letters between buildings.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling a switch an L3 device. L2 switches forward by MAC; "L3 switches" also route in hardware.
  • Forgetting the MAC table is finite (a few thousand to 100k+ entries); MAC flooding fills it and turns the switch into a hub.

notes.title: VLANs and broadcast domains
notes.html:
A broadcast domain is every device that hears a broadcast (like ARP). A VLAN splits one physical switch into several isolated broadcast domains. Frames get a 4-byte 802.1Q tag with a 12-bit VLAN ID (1 to 4094). Access ports carry one VLAN untagged; trunk ports carry many tagged VLANs.

Different VLANs talk only through a router (inter-VLAN routing, "router on a stick" or an L3 switch SVI).

Worked example. 1,000 hosts on one flat L2 produce thousands of ARP and broadcast packets per second that every host must process. Splitting into four /24 VLANs of 250 hosts cuts broadcast load about 4x and limits the blast radius of a loop.

Industry examples. Cloud networks avoid VLAN limits (4,094) with VXLAN (24-bit VNI, 16M segments), used by AWS-like overlays, Kubernetes CNIs (Flannel, Calico VXLAN mode) and VMware NSX.

Decision gravity. Segmentation by VLAN is cheap and reversible, but stretching L2 across data centers is risky (loops, storms). Modern DCs route (L3) to the top-of-rack switch and overlay L2 on top where needed.

Everyday analogy. Floors of a building: a shout on floor 2 is not heard on floor 5; to talk across floors you use the lift (router).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing VLANs are security by themselves; misconfigured trunks allow VLAN hopping.
  • Not knowing spanning tree (STP) exists to stop L2 loops, which otherwise cause broadcast storms that take the network down in seconds.

notes.title: How a router decides: routing tables
notes.html:
A router holds a table of prefixes and picks the most specific match (longest prefix match). Each entry says "for destination X/n, send to next hop Y out of interface Z".

$ ip route
default via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0
10.0.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.0.15
10.0.1.0/24 via 10.0.0.2 dev eth0
10.0.1.128/25 via 10.0.0.3 dev eth0

Packet to 10.0.1.200: matches 10.0.1.0/24 (24 bits) and 10.0.1.128/25 (25 bits, longer); the /25 wins, so next hop 10.0.0.3. Packet to 8.8.8.8 matches only default (0.0.0.0/0).

Routes arrive three ways: connected (the interface's own subnet), static (an admin typed it), dynamic (learned from protocols). When multiple sources offer the same prefix, administrative distance picks (connected 0, static 1, OSPF 110, RIP 120, eBGP 20 on Cisco-style devices).

Worked example. Core internet routers hold ~1 million IPv4 prefixes in specialised memory (TCAM); lookup happens in a few nanoseconds in hardware. Software routers use tries.

Industry examples. Cloud route tables (AWS VPC) work this way: 0.0.0.0/0 -> igw-xxx makes a subnet public, -> nat-xxx makes it private, 10.1.0.0/16 -> pcx-xxx sends to a peered VPC; the most specific route wins.

Everyday analogy. A GPS-less driver following signs: "Mumbai" sign vs "Mumbai Andheri" sign: you follow the more specific one.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting longest prefix match and explaining by order of rules.
  • Missing the return route: a ping works one way, fails the other because the far side has no route back.
  • Asymmetric routing breaking stateful firewalls.

notes.title: Interior routing: OSPF, RIP and data center routing
notes.html:
Inside one organisation (an autonomous system), routers learn routes from each other by an interior gateway protocol (IGP).

  • RIP: distance-vector, counts hops (max 15). Simple, slow, obsolete.
  • OSPF: link-state; every router floods its links to all others, each runs Dijkstra to build the map. Fast convergence, scales to hundreds of routers in areas. Cost depends on bandwidth.
  • IS-IS: similar link-state, favoured by ISPs.
  • Data center fabrics: often eBGP in leaf-spine (Meta, Microsoft), since BGP handles huge scale and policy.

Worked example (convergence). A link fails. OSPF with default timers (hello 10 s, dead 40 s) takes up to 40 s to notice; with BFD (bidirectional forwarding detection) at 50 ms x 3 detection is ~150 ms. Tuning detection time is the main lever.

Industry examples. Calico can peer pods with the data center via BGP; Kubernetes pod routes advertised so no overlay is needed. Cilium offers BGP control plane too.

Decision gravity. Choosing a routing protocol is mostly a one-way door at the fabric level (changing it means a migration); for small networks static routes are simpler and fine.

Everyday analogy. Every taxi driver in a city sharing the live traffic map (link-state) versus asking neighbours "how far are you from the airport?" (distance vector).

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up "IGP inside an AS" and "BGP between ASes".
  • Forgetting that dynamic routing can loop briefly during convergence; the TTL field is the safety net.

notes.title: BGP: how the internet is stitched together
notes.html:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is how autonomous systems tell each other which IP prefixes they can reach. Each AS has a number (ASN): Google 15169, Cloudflare 13335, AWS 16509 (AS14618 also). A router advertises "I can reach 8.8.8.0/24 via AS path [15169]"; neighbours prepend their own ASN and pass it on. The AS path is also loop protection (a router drops a route containing its own ASN).

BGP is a path-vector protocol that runs over TCP port 179, driven by policy (money and contracts), not shortest distance. Rough order of best path selection: highest local preference, shortest AS path, lowest origin type, lowest MED, eBGP over iBGP, lowest IGP cost.

Relationships between ASes:

  • Customer to provider (transit): the customer pays for access to the whole internet.
  • Peer to peer: two ASes swap traffic for each other's customers free (at an Internet Exchange like AMS-IX, DE-CIX, NIXI in India).
  • Rule of thumb ("valley-free"): don't give free transit; ASes advertise customer routes to everybody, but peer and provider routes only to customers.
# Looking-glass style view of a route
$ whois -h whois.radb.net 8.8.8.0/24
route:   8.8.8.0/24
origin:  AS15169
$ birdc show route for 8.8.8.8 all     # on a BIRD router
8.8.8.0/24 via 198.51.100.2 [bgp 12:00] * (100) [AS15169i]
        BGP.as_path: 3356 15169

Worked example. Internet shape: about 75,000+ active ASNs and ~1 million IPv4 routes (2024 to 2025 figures; confirm current). A global router full table takes about 1 to 2 GB RAM on software routers.

Real incidents. (1) 2008: Pakistan Telecom announced a more specific YouTube prefix to block it locally and leaked it, blackholing YouTube worldwide for ~2 hours. (2) 2021: Facebook withdrew its prefixes during a bad maintenance command, so its DNS and services disappeared; internal tools also died. (3) 2019: a small ISP's route leak via Verizon took out chunks of Cloudflare and AWS traffic. Mitigations: RPKI route origin validation (ROAs), prefix filters, max-prefix limits, MANRS.

Decision gravity. Becoming multi-homed (two upstreams) buys resilience and is reversible per link; announcing your own prefixes needs an ASN and PI address space (a registry process, hard to undo). BGP has no built-in security; RPKI adoption is gradual.

Everyday analogy. Airlines code-sharing: each airline only tells partners where it flies; you choose by price and agreements, not the shortest flight.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying BGP picks the fastest route. It follows business policy and AS path length.
  • Forgetting eBGP vs iBGP; iBGP does not change the AS path.
  • Not knowing that more specific prefixes win, which is how hijacks work.

notes.title: The internet's structure: tiers, IXPs and CDNs
notes.html:
The internet is a loose hierarchy plus a lot of direct shortcuts.

  • Tier 1 networks (Lumen, Arelion, NTT, Tata Communications, etc.) can reach every route without paying anyone; they peer with each other.
  • Tier 2 / regional ISPs buy transit and also peer.
  • Access ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Comcast) serve homes and phones.
  • IXPs are switches where many networks connect and peer cheaply (DE-CIX in Frankfurt peaks above 14 Tbps).
  • Content networks (Google, Netflix, Meta, Akamai, Cloudflare) peer directly with access ISPs or place caches inside them, so most traffic never touches Tier 1 carriers.

Worked example (cost). Video from a faraway origin: transit costs maybe $0.50 to $2 per Mbps per month at scale. Netflix at 20 Tbps average would pay a fortune, so Open Connect boxes inside ISPs cut transit to near zero for 90%+ of its bytes.

Industry examples. Google's Espresso/Edge peering and its private subsea cables (Dunant, Equiano); Meta and Microsoft cable consortia. About 95%+ of international data crosses roughly 500+ submarine cables.

Decision gravity. Where you peer or place PoPs is a long-term contract choice. Using a cloud's backbone (e.g. AWS Global Accelerator, Cloudflare Argo) is rentable and reversible.

Everyday analogy. Highways (Tier 1), state roads (regional), local streets (access) and private expressways that big companies built to their own warehouses (content networks).

Common interview traps.

  • Describing only a strict hierarchy; the flat peering model is what dominates today.
  • Not knowing what an IXP is.

notes.title: Latency vs distance
notes.html:
Latency is delay, bandwidth is capacity. Latency has a physical floor: light in fibre goes about 200 km per millisecond (about 5 microseconds per km). RTT floor = 2 x distance / 200 km per ms. Real RTTs are 1.5x to 2x that, because cables are not straight and routers add delay.

Route Great-circle distance Floor RTT Typical real RTT
Same city 20 km 0.2 ms 1 to 5 ms
Mumbai to Delhi 1,150 km 11.5 ms 20 to 30 ms
Mumbai to Singapore 3,900 km 39 ms 55 to 70 ms
Mumbai to Frankfurt 6,500 km 65 ms 110 to 130 ms
Mumbai to New York 12,500 km 125 ms 180 to 220 ms
Geostationary satellite 2 x 35,786 km up ~480 ms 600+ ms (Starlink LEO: 25 to 60 ms)

Latency components: propagation (distance/speed), transmission (size / bandwidth: 1,500 B at 10 Mbps = 1.2 ms), queuing (bufferbloat, can be hundreds of ms), processing (routers, TLS, app).

Worked example (bandwidth-delay product). 1 Gbps link with 100 ms RTT holds 1 Gbps x 0.1 s = 100 Mbit = 12.5 MB in flight. A TCP connection needs a window at least that large to fill the pipe; otherwise throughput = window / RTT. A 64 KB window at 100 ms RTT gives 64 KB / 0.1 s = 640 KB/s (about 5 Mbps) on a 1 Gbps link, which is why long fat networks need window scaling (see TCP notes).

Fixes ranked. (1) Move data closer: CDN, edge cache, regional DB replicas. (2) Fewer round trips: keep-alive, HTTP/2 or 3, batching, TLS 1.3 / 0-RTT, GraphQL or aggregated APIs. (3) Parallelise. (4) Compress to cut transfer time. You cannot buy a faster speed of light.

mtr -rwc 50 -n example.com          # see per-hop latency and loss
ping -c 10 -i 0.2 host              # jitter from mdev
curl -w "connect:%{time_connect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer}\n" -so /dev/null https://host

Industry examples. Cloud multi-region design (DynamoDB global tables, Spanner) is a trade of consistency against cross-region RTT (US to EU ~80 to 100 ms). High-frequency traders pay millions for microwave links between Chicago and New Jersey (about 3.9 ms one way versus ~6.5 ms on fibre). WhatsApp and Cloudflare terminate TCP/TLS near users to shorten handshakes.

Everyday analogy. Water in a long pipe: wide pipe (bandwidth) lets lots flow at once, but the first drop still takes time to arrive (latency).

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing bandwidth with latency: a faster plan does not reduce RTT.
  • Forgetting a request chain of N sequential calls over 100 ms RTT costs N x 100 ms (chatty APIs).
  • Quoting averages; p99 latency is what users feel.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Switches forward frames by MAC inside a network; routers forward packets by IP between networks, using longest prefix match.
  • VLANs and L3 boundaries limit broadcast domains; STP prevents L2 loops.
  • IGPs (OSPF, IS-IS) run inside an AS; BGP is the path-vector, policy-driven protocol between ASes over TCP 179.
  • BGP trust problems cause leaks and hijacks (YouTube 2008, Facebook 2021); RPKI and filters mitigate them.
  • The internet is flatter now: IXPs, direct peering and CDN caches inside ISPs.
  • Latency floor is about 1 ms RTT per 100 km of fibre; bandwidth-delay product decides window sizes; the main fix is moving data closer and cutting round trips.
